desc:
A browser starts on the page with id home. It keeps a history of the visited pages as a doubly linked chain and a current position in that chain. Each operation is a pair [type, x]:

  • [0, page]: visit page. All pages after the current position (the forward history) are discarded, the new page is appended and becomes current.
  • [1, steps]: go back up to steps pages. You stop early at the oldest page of the history.
  • [2, steps]: go forward up to steps pages. You stop early at the newest page of the history.

Return an array with the id of the current page after every operation. For example with home = 1 and ops = [[0,2],[0,3],[1,1],[2,5],[1,5],[0,9]] the answer is [2,3,2,3,1,9]: after visiting 2 and 3 the history is 1,2,3; going back 1 gives 2, forward 5 stops at 3, back 5 stops at 1, and visiting 9 replaces the forward history so it becomes 1,9.
constraints: Visited page ids and home are in the range 1..10<sup>9</sup>; the same page may be visited many times
hints: A history in which you move one step at a time in both directions is exactly a doubly linked list with a 'current' pointer.
A visit creates a new node after the current one, and simply throws the old forward part away by overwriting cur.next.

For back and forward, follow prev or next pointers while the step counter lasts and the pointer exists. Output cur.val after every operation. (An array with an index and a 'length' that you shrink on visit also works.)
editorial: Model the history as a doubly linked list. Keep a pointer cur. Visiting creates a node n, sets cur.next = n, n.prev = cur and moves cur to n; the old forward nodes become unreachable at once because nothing points to them any more.

Moving back or forward walks at most steps links but stops at the ends. A single move costs O(min(steps, length)), so the total is O(q · n) in the worst case, which is fine here. An equivalent approach stores pages in an array, keeps the current index and the logical length, and on a visit overwrites the slot after the index; then back and forward are O(1) index arithmetic with clamping.
